title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 847–848 (Night 191, continuing nights-190), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 191 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. The prince tests his father's disbelief with an example: has anyone ever dreamed of fighting and woken with a bloodied sword in his hand? He then tells again the whole story of that night — the girl asleep beside him, as tall and as fair as himself, the rings they exchanged, how he held back from kissing her for shame, fearing his father had sent her to test him and was hiding to watch — and holds out her ring on his little finger as proof. King Shahramān turns the ring over, owns that there is a great story behind it, blames the vizier for the whole trouble, and urges patience with a verse of hope; he now grants that his son is not mad. Qamar al-Zamān begs him to find the girl quickly or he will die of grief, recites two lines on the phantom that cannot visit a sleepless lover, and turns to his father in tears to recite more, and dawn overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْحَادِيَةُ وَالتِّسْعُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-ḥādiyatu wa-al-tisʿūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the first and the ninety after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and ninety-first night,
sentences.n: Last night needed the formula for a round number (al-mūfiya li-al-tisʿīn, “the one completing the ninety”); with a unit in front the plain pattern returns: al-ḥādiya, “the first”, the ordinal used for “one” inside a compound number, feminine to agree with layla; then wa-al-tisʿūna, “and the ninety”, in its cardinal form; then baʿda al-miʾa, “after the hundred”. The ئ of المائة is printed, and its alif is silent: the word is miʾa.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ قَالَ لِوَالِدِهِ أَنَا أَضْرِبُ لَكَ مَثَلًا يُبَيِّنُ لَكَ أَنَّ هٰذَا كَانَ فِى الْيَقْظَةِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Qamara al-Zamāni qāla li-wālidihi anā aḍribu laka mathalan yubayyinu laka anna hādhā kāna fī al-yaqẓati
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that Qamar al-Zamān said to-his-father: I, I-strike for-you a-likeness (that) makes-clear to-you that this was in the-waking.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that Qamar al-Zamān said to his father, “I will give you an example that will show you this happened while I was awake.
sentences.n: Shahrazād takes up the story with the very sentence that ended the last night. ḍaraba mathalan, “to strike a likeness”, to give an example; yubayyinu, Form II, “to make plain”, an unmarked relative clause after the indefinite mathalan; its shadda is printed. Qamara al-Zamāni is accusative as the noun of anna.

sentences.t: وَهُوَ أَنِّي أَسْأَلُكَ هَلِ اتَّفَقَ لِأَحَدٍ أَنَّهُ رَأَى نَفْسَهُ فِى الْمَنَامِ يُقَاتِلُ وَقَدْ قَاتَلَ قِتَالًا شَدِيدًا
sentences.tr: wa-huwa annī asʾaluka hali ittafaqa li-aḥadin annahu raʾā nafsahu fī al-manāmi yuqātilu wa-qad qātala qitālan shadīdan
sentences.l: And-it (is) that-I ask-you: did it-happen to-anyone that-he saw himself in the-sleep fighting, and-indeed he-fought a-fighting fierce,
sentences.i: It is this: I ask you, has it ever happened to anyone that he saw himself fighting in his sleep, and fought a hard fight,
sentences.n: wa-huwa annī …, “and it is that I …”: huwa points forward to the example about to be given. ittafaqa li-, Form VIII, “to happen to”: li- marks the one it befalls. hal takes a helping kasra, hali, because the first vowel of ittafaqa drops after it and two unvowelled consonants would otherwise meet. yuqātilu, “fighting”, describes what he saw himself doing. qātala qitālan shadīdan, “fought a fierce fighting”: the verb’s own verbal noun as object, the cognate accusative that strengthens it. The hamza of the second alif of اسألك, and of رأى, are printed.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ اسْتَيْقَظَ مِنْ مَنَامِهِ فَوَجَدَ فِي يَدِهِ سَيْفًا مُلَوَّثًا بِالدَّمِ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda dhālika istayqaẓa min manāmihi fa-wajada fī yadihi sayfan mulawwathan bi-al-dami
sentences.l: and-after that he-woke from his-sleep and-found in his-hand a-sword smeared with-the-blood?
sentences.i: and afterwards woke from his sleep and found in his hand a sword stained with blood?”
sentences.n: istayqaẓa, Form X of yaqiẓa, “to wake”. mulawwath, Form II passive participle, “smeared, stained”; its shadda is printed, and bi- marks what it is smeared with. The point of the question: a dream leaves nothing behind in the hand.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ وَالِدُهُ لَا وَاللَّهِ يَا وَلَدِي لَمْ يَتَّفِقْ هٰذَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu wāliduhu lā wa-Allāhi yā waladī lam yattafiq hādhā
sentences.l: So-said to-him his-father: No, by-God, O my-son, not happened this.
sentences.i: His father said to him, “No, by God, my son, that has never happened.”
sentences.n: lā wa-Allāhi, “no, by God”: the denial comes first and the oath backs it. lam with the jussive, yattafiq, negates the past; its shadda is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ لِوَالِدِهِ أَنَا أُخْبِرُكَ بِمَا حَصَلَ لِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Qamaru al-Zamāni li-wālidihi anā ukhbiruka bi-mā ḥaṣala lī
sentences.l: So-said Qamar al-Zamān to-his-father: I, I-inform-you of-what befell to-me.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān said to his father, “I will tell you what happened to me.
sentences.n: akhbara bi-, Form IV, “to tell (someone) of”: bi- marks the thing told, here bi-mā, “of what”. ḥaṣala li-, “to happen to”, a verb much used in this later prose.

sentences.t: وَهُوَ أَنِّي رَأَيْتُ فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ كَأَنِّي اسْتَيْقَظْتُ مِنْ مَنَامِي نِصْفَ اللَّيْلِ فَوَجَدْتُ بِنْتًا نَائِمَةً بِجَانِبِي قَدُّهَا كَقَدِّي وَشَكْلُهَا كَشَكْلِي
sentences.tr: wa-huwa annī raʾaytu fī hādhihi al-laylati kaʾannī istayqaẓtu min manāmī niṣfa al-layli fa-wajadtu bintan nāʾimatan bi-jānibī qadduhā ka-qaddī wa-shakluhā ka-shaklī
sentences.l: And-it (is) that-I saw in this the-night as-if-I woke from my-sleep (at) half (of) the-night, and-I-found a-girl sleeping at-my-side, her-stature like-my-stature and-her-form like-my-form.
sentences.i: It is this: tonight it seemed to me that I woke from my sleep at midnight and found a girl asleep beside me, her figure like my figure and her looks like my looks.
sentences.n: raʾaytu … kaʾannī, “I saw as though I …”, is the ordinary way of telling a dream, and the prince uses it even while insisting that this was none. niṣfa al-layli, “at midnight”, an accusative of time. bi-jānibī, “at my side”: bi- of place. qadd, “stature, figure”, a favourite word of the love poets; ka-, “like”, governs the genitive. The shadda of كقدّي is printed, and so are the hamza of رأيت and كأني and the ئ of نائمة. The rhyme qaddī / shaklī ends the sentence.

sentences.t: فَعَانَقْتُهَا وَقَلَّبْتُهَا بِيَدِي وَأَخَذْتُ خَاتَمَهَا وَلَبِسْتُهُ فِي إِصْبَعِي
sentences.tr: fa-ʿānaqtuhā wa-qallabtuhā bi-yadī wa-akhadhtu khātamahā wa-labistuhu fī iṣbaʿī
sentences.l: So-I-embraced-her and-turned-her-over with-my-hand, and-I-took her-ring and-put-it-on on my-finger,
sentences.i: I embraced her and turned her this way and that with my hand, and took her ring and put it on my finger,
sentences.n: ʿānaqa, Form III, “to embrace”. qallaba, Form II, “to turn over and over”; bi-yadī, “with my hand”, bi- of the instrument. The damma of اخذتُ is printed. labisa, “to put on, wear”, of a ring as of clothes. iṣbaʿ, “finger”, a word with many vocalisations (uṣbuʿ, aṣbaʿ and others).

sentences.t: وَقَلَعْتُ خَاتَمِي وَأَلْبَسْتُهُ فِي إِصْبَعِهَا وَنِمْتُ بِجَنْبِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-qalaʿtu khātamī wa-albastuhu fī iṣbaʿihā wa-nimtu bi-janbihā
sentences.l: and-I-pulled-off my-ring and-made-(her)-wear-it on her-finger, and-I-slept at-her-side.
sentences.i: and drew off my own ring and put it on her finger, and slept beside her.
sentences.n: qalaʿa, “to pull out, pull off”. labistuhu, “I put it on (myself)”, and albastuhu, Form IV, “I put it on (her)”: the plain verb and its causative show the exchange of rings. nimtu, “I slept”, from nāma, the long ā shortening to i before the ending. janb and jānib, both “side”, the second a moment ago.

sentences.t: وَامْتَنَعْتُ عَنْهَا حَيَاءً مِنْكَ وَخَوْفًا أَنْ تَكُونَ أَنْتَ أَرْسَلْتَهَا تَمْتَحِنُنِي بِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-imtanaʿtu ʿanhā ḥayāʾan minka wa-khawfan an takūna anta arsaltahā tamtaḥinunī bihā
sentences.l: And-I-held-back from-her (out of) shame from-you and-(out of) fear that you-be you sent-her, you-test-me with-her,
sentences.i: But I kept myself from her, out of shame before you, and for fear that you yourself had sent her to test me with her,
sentences.n: imtanaʿa ʿan, Form VIII, “to hold back from”. ḥayāʾan and khawfan are accusatives of cause, “out of shame, out of fear”; ḥayāʾ min, “shame before (someone)”. arsaltahā tamtaḥinunī, “you sent her, you test me”: an imperfect of purpose with no link, as the king’s arsaltu ākhudhuhā in the last night. imtaḥana bi-, “to test with”: bi- marks the means of the test.

sentences.t: وَظَنَنْتُ أَنَّكَ مُخْتَفِي فِي مَكَانٍ لِتَنْظُرَ مَا أَفْعَلُ بِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-ẓanantu annaka mukhtafī fī makānin li-tanẓura mā afʿalu bihā
sentences.l: and-I-thought that-you (were) hidden in a-place so-that-you-see what I-do with-her;
sentences.i: and I thought you were hidden somewhere to see what I would do with her;
sentences.n: mukhtafī, participle of ikhtafā, Form VIII, “to hide oneself”: Classical Arabic writes it mukhtafin, dropping the yāʾ, when it has neither article nor suffix; the print keeps the yāʾ, as later Arabic does, and it is read so. li- with the subjunctive, “so that”. faʿala bi-, “to do with, do to”.

sentences.t: وَاسْتَحْيَيْتُ مِنْ أَجْلِ ذٰلِكَ أَنْ أُقَبِّلَهَا فِي فَمِهَا حَيَاءً مِنْكَ
sentences.tr: wa-istaḥyaytu min ajli dhālika an uqabbilahā fī famihā ḥayāʾan minka
sentences.l: and-I-was-ashamed because-of that to kiss-her on her-mouth, (out of) shame from-you.
sentences.i: and so I was too ashamed to kiss her on the mouth, for shame before you.
sentences.n: istaḥyā, Form X of the root of ḥayāʾ, “to be too bashful (to do something)”, with an and the subjunctive for the thing one shrinks from. min ajli, “for the sake of, because of”. qabbala fī, “to kiss on”; the shadda of اقبّلها is printed. The prince’s story repeats itself, ḥayāʾan minka for the second time.

sentences.t: وَظَنَنْتُ أَنَّكَ تُرَغِّبُنِي فِى الزَّوَاجِ
sentences.tr: wa-ẓanantu annaka turaghghibunī fī al-zawāji
sentences.l: And-I-thought that-you (were) making-me-desire in the-marriage.
sentences.i: I thought you meant to give me a liking for marriage.
sentences.n: The damma of ظننتُ is printed. ترغبني is read, as the sense seems to ask, as turaghghibunī, Form II, “to make (someone) desire (fī) something”, though the print sets no shadda; the plain verb, targhabunī, “you desire me”, makes no sense here. raghiba fī, “to desire”: fī marks the thing wanted.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ انْتَبَهْتُ مِنْ مَنَامِي فِي وَجْهِ الصُّبْحِ فَلَمْ أَجِدْ لِلصَّبِيَّةِ أَثَرًا وَلَا وَقَفْتُ لَهَا عَلَى خَبَرٍ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda dhālika intabahtu min manāmī fī wajhi al-ṣubḥi fa-lam ajid li-al-ṣabiyyati atharan wa-lā waqaftu lahā ʿalā khabarin
sentences.l: And-after that I-awoke from my-sleep in (the) face (of) the-morning, and-not I-found of-the-girl a-trace, nor came-I for-her upon news.
sentences.i: After that I woke from my sleep at first light and found no trace of the girl, nor could I come on any word of her.
sentences.n: intabaha, Form VIII, “to wake, come to oneself”; the damma of انتبهتُ is printed. fī wajhi al-ṣubḥi, “in the face of the morning”, at first light. lam ajid, jussive after lam; li-al-ṣabiyyati, “of the girl”, li- of belonging, with the shadda of the print. waqafa ʿalā, “to come upon, find out”; lā with the perfect continues the past denial of lam. The rhyme: atharan / khabarin.

sentences.t: وَجَرَى لِي مَعَ الْخَادِمِ وَالْوَزِيرِ مَا جَرَى فَكَيْفَ يَكُونُ هٰذَا الْأَمْرُ مَنَامًا وَكَذِبًا وَأَمْرُ الْخَاتَمِ صَحِيحٌ
sentences.tr: wa-jarā lī maʿa al-khādimi wa-al-wazīri mā jarā fa-kayfa yakūnu hādhā al-amru manāman wa-kadhiban wa-amru al-khātami ṣaḥīḥun
sentences.l: And-ran to-me with the-servant and-the-vizier what ran. So-how is this the-matter a-dream and-a-lie, while-(the)-matter (of) the-ring (is) sound?
sentences.i: Then there passed between me and the servant and the vizier what passed. So how can this be a dream and a lie, when the ring is real?
sentences.n: jarā li- … mā jarā, “there happened to me what happened”, the storyteller’s way of not retelling what the hearer knows: here, the prince’s violent handling of the servant and the vizier in the nights before. wa-amru al-khātami ṣaḥīḥun, a circumstantial clause, “while the matter of the ring is sound”. kadhib (also kidhb), “lie”, accusative like manāman as the predicate of yakūnu.

sentences.t: وَلَوْلَا الْخَاتَمُ كُنْتُ أَظُنُّ أَنَّهُ مَنَامٌ
sentences.tr: wa-lawlā al-khātamu kuntu aẓunnu annahu manāmun
sentences.l: And-were-it-not-for the-ring, I-was thinking that-it (was) a-dream.
sentences.i: Were it not for the ring, I would think it a dream.
sentences.n: lawlā, “were it not for”, takes a noun in the nominative. Classical Arabic marks the answer with la-, la-kuntu; the print has plain kuntu, common in later prose.

sentences.t: وَهٰذَا خَاتَمُهَا فِي خِنْصِرِي فَانْظُرْ أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ إِلَى الْخَاتَمِ كَمْ يُسَاوِي
sentences.tr: wa-hādhā khātamuhā fī khinṣirī fa-unẓur ayyuhā al-maliku ilā al-khātami kam yusāwī
sentences.l: And-this (is) her-ring on my-little-finger; so-look, O king, at the-ring, how-much it-is-worth!
sentences.i: Here is her ring on my little finger. Look at the ring, O king, and see what it is worth!”
sentences.n: khinṣir, “little finger”, also said khinṣar. naẓara ilā, “to look at”: ilā marks what is looked at. kam yusāwī, “how much it is worth”, from sāwā, Form III, “to be equal to”. The son now addresses his father as ayyuhā al-malik, “O king”, as one appealing to a judge.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ نَاوَلَ الْخَاتَمَ لِأَبِيهِ فَأَخَذَهُ وَتَأَمَّلَهُ وَقَلَّبَهُ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Qamara al-Zamāni nāwala al-khātama li-abīhi fa-akhadhahu wa-taʾammalahu wa-qallabahu
sentences.l: Then indeed Qamar al-Zamān handed the-ring to-his-father, and-he-took-it and-examined-it and-turned-it-over.
sentences.i: Then Qamar al-Zamān handed the ring to his father, who took it, looked at it closely and turned it this way and that.
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then (it was) that”, the narrator’s link between scenes; the noun after inna is accusative. nāwala, Form III, “to hand”: Classical Arabic says nāwalahu al-khātama, “handed him the ring”, and li- for the receiver is later usage. abīhi, genitive of ab, “father”, which lengthens its vowel before a suffix. taʾammala, Form V, “to look at closely”; the shadda of تامّله and of قلّبه are printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ الْتَفَتَ إِلَى وَلَدِهِ وَقٰلَ لَهُ إِنَّ لِهٰذَا الْخَاتَمِ نَبَأً عَظِيمًا وَخَبَرًا جَسِيمًا
sentences.tr: thumma iltafata ilā waladihi wa-qāla lahu inna li-hādhā al-khātami nabaʾan ʿaẓīman wa-khabaran jasīman
sentences.l: Then he-turned to his-son and-said to-him: Indeed to-this the-ring (is) a-tidings great and-a-news weighty,
sentences.i: Then he turned to his son and said to him, “There is a great story to this ring, and a weighty one,
sentences.n: The print spells qāla defectively, قل, pointed here with the dagger alif. iltafata ilā, Form VIII, “to turn to”. inna li-hādhā …, “this ring has”: li- of possession, with the thing possessed coming after and taking the accusative of inna. nabaʾ and khabar, both “news, tidings”, paired in rhyme, ʿaẓīman / jasīman. The hamza of نبأ is printed.

sentences.t: وَإِنَّ الَّذِي اتَّفَقَ لَكَ فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ مَعَ تِلْكَ الصَّبِيَّةِ أَمْرٌ مُشْكِلٌ
sentences.tr: wa-inna alladhī ittafaqa laka fī hādhihi al-laylati maʿa tilka al-ṣabiyyati amrun mushkilun
sentences.l: and-indeed that-which happened to-you in this the-night with that the-girl (is) a-matter obscure.
sentences.i: and what befell you tonight with that girl is a puzzling business.
sentences.n: mushkil, Form IV participle, “hard to make out, obscure”. The shadda of الصبيّة is printed.

sentences.t: وَلَا أَعْلَمُ مِنْ أَيْنَ دَخَلَ عَلَيْنَا هٰذَا الدَّخِيلُ وَمَا سَبَبُ هٰذِهِ الْفِتْنَةِ كُلِّهَا إِلَّا الْوَزِيرُ
sentences.tr: wa-lā aʿlamu min ayna dakhala ʿalaynā hādhā al-dakhīlu wa-mā sababu hādhihi al-fitnati kullihā illā al-wazīru
sentences.l: And-not I-know from where entered upon-us this the-intruder, and-not (is the) cause (of) this the-trouble, all-of-it, except the-vizier.
sentences.i: I do not know from where this intruder came in upon us; and the cause of all this trouble is none but the vizier.
sentences.n: dakhala ʿalā, “to come in upon (someone)”, and al-dakhīl, “the one who comes in”, the intruder: a play on one root. mā … illā, “nothing but”: after the negation the excepted noun keeps the case the clause gives it, so al-wazīru, the predicate, is nominative. fitna, “trouble, trial, discord”. kullihā, “all of it”, agrees with al-fitnati in the genitive. The king lays the blame on the vizier, as he has before.

sentences.t: فَبِاللَّهِ عَلَيْكَ يَا وَلَدِي اصْبِرْ حَتَّى يُفَرِّجَ اللَّهُ عَنْكَ هٰذِهِ الْكُرْبَةَ وَيَأْتِيَكَ بِالْفَرَجِ الْعَظِيمِ فَإِنَّ بَعْضَ الشُّعَرَاءِ قَالَ
sentences.tr: fa-bi-Allāhi ʿalayka yā waladī iṣbir ḥattā yufarrija Allāhu ʿanka hādhihi al-kurbata wa-yaʾtiyaka bi-al-faraji al-ʿaẓīmi fa-inna baʿḍa al-shuʿarāʾi qāla
sentences.l: So-by-God (I-adjure)-upon-you, O my-son, be-patient until God relieves from-you this the-distress and-brings-you the-relief the-great; for indeed some (of) the-poets said:
sentences.i: I adjure you by God, my son, be patient until God lifts this distress from you and brings you great relief; for one of the poets has said:
sentences.n: The print has ويأنيك, a misprint for ويأتيك, corrected here. bi-Allāhi ʿalayka, the formula of earnest entreaty met in the last night. farraja ʿan, Form II, “to lift (a burden) from (someone)”: the burden is the object, and ʿan marks the one set free. ḥattā, “until”, takes the subjunctive, and the second verb, joined by wa-, shares it: yaʾtiyaka. atā bi-, “to bring”: the verb takes the thing brought with bi-, so yaʾtiyaka bi-al-faraji, “bring you relief”. kurba and faraj, “distress” and “relief”, are a stock pair. baʿḍa al-shuʿarāʾi, “some of the poets”, accusative after inna, that is, a certain poet. The hamza of يأتيك is printed.

sentences.t:
عَسَى وَلَعَلَّ الدَّهْرُ يَلْوِي عِنَانَهُ * وَيَأْتِي بِخَيْرٍ فَالزَّمَانُ غَيُورُ
وَتُسْعِدُ آمَالِي وَتَقْضِي حَوَائِجِي * وَتَحْدُثُ مِنْ بَعْدِ الْاُمُوْرِ اُمُوْرُ
sentences.tr:
ʿasā wa-laʿalla al-dahru yalwī ʿinānahu * wa-yaʾtī bi-khayrin fa-al-zamānu ghayūru
wa-tusʿidu āmālī wa-taqḍī ḥawāʾijī * wa-taḥduthu min baʿdi al-umūri umūru
sentences.l:
Perhaps, and-maybe, the-Time twists its-rein * and-brings good, for-the-Time (is) jealous;
and-favours my-hopes and-fulfils my-needs, * and-there-happen from after the-affairs affairs.
sentences.i:
It may be, it may well be, that Time will turn its rein * and bring some good, for Time is jealous and will not stay;
and favour my hopes, and see my needs fulfilled, * for after some things happen, other things come about.
sentences.n: The print points the verse, and its pointing is kept. ʿasā and laʿalla, both “perhaps”, are heaped up for hope; laʿalla would put al-dahr in the accusative, but the print gives al-dahru the nominative, which fits it as the subject of ʿasā. lawā ʿinānahu, “to twist its rein”, to wheel round as a rider turns his horse: Time may turn back toward the speaker. atā bi-, “to bring”, as in the prose just before. ghayūr, “jealous”: Time grudges men their happiness and so never holds one course, which is the poet’s ground for hope. In the second line tusʿidu and taqḍī are feminine (or second person) though dahr is masculine; the poet seems to let fortune in general be their subject. taḥduthu agrees with umūr, a broken plural. The last half-line recalls the Qurʾān, “perhaps God will bring about (yuḥdithu) after that a new matter” (Sūrat al-Ṭalāq 65:1). The print writes the hamza of al-umūr and umūr as a damma on bare alif and sets a sukūn on their long ū, its usual verse habit; umūru at the line’s end goes without tanwīn, as rhyme allows.

sentences.t: فَيَا وَلَدِي إِنِّي تَحَقَّقْتُ فِي هٰذِهِ السَّاعَةِ أَنْ مَابِكَ جُنُونٌ وَلٰكِنَّ قِصَّتَكَ غَرِيبَةٌ لَا يُجَلِّيهَا عَنْكَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ تَعَالَى
sentences.tr: fa-yā waladī innī taḥaqqaqtu fī hādhihi al-sāʿati an mā bika junūnun wa-lākinna qiṣṣataka gharībatun lā yujallīhā ʿanka illā Allāhu taʿālā
sentences.l: So-O my-son, indeed-I made-sure in this the-hour that not in-you (is) madness, but your-story (is) strange; not clears-it-away from-you except God, (He is) exalted.
sentences.i: My son, I am now certain that there is no madness in you; but your story is a strange one, and none but God Most High can clear it up for you.”
sentences.n: The print sets ما and بك together, مابك; the spacing is kept. an is read as the lightened form of anna, which can take a whole clause, here a negated one: mā bika junūnun, “there is no madness in you”, with bi- “in” of what afflicts a person. The other reading, anna mā bika junūnun, would mean “that what ails you is madness”, the opposite of what the king now concedes. taḥaqqaqa, Form V, “to make sure, be certain”. jallā ʿan, Form II, “to clear (a thing) away from”; the shadda of يجلّيها is printed. Allāhu taʿālā, “God, exalted (is He)”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ بِاللَّهِ يَا وَالِدِي إِنَّكَ تَفْعَلُ مَعِي جَمِيلًا وَتَفْحَصُ لِي عَنْ هٰذِهِ الصَّبِيَّةِ وَتُعَجِّلُ بِقُدُومِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Qamaru al-Zamāni bi-Allāhi yā wālidī innaka tafʿalu maʿī jamīlan wa-tafḥaṣu lī ʿan hādhihi al-ṣabiyyati wa-tuʿajjilu bi-qudūmihā
sentences.l: So-said to-him Qamar al-Zamān: By-God, O my-father, indeed-you do with-me a-kindness and-search for-me about this the-girl and-hasten her-coming,
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān said to him, “By God, father, do me a kindness: search out this girl for me and hasten her coming,
sentences.n: After an oath of entreaty, innaka tafʿalu, “you will surely do”, serves as a polite command: the favour is spoken of as though already granted. faʿala maʿahu jamīlan, “to do someone a kindness”, jamīl being “a fair deed”. faḥaṣa ʿan, “to search into, inquire after”: ʿan marks what is sought, and lī, “for me”, the one it is done for. ʿajjala bi-, Form II, “to hasten (something)”: bi- marks the thing hastened; the shadda of تعجّل and of الصبيّة are printed. qudūm, “arrival, coming”.

sentences.t: وَإِلَّامُتُّ كَمَدًا لَمْ يَدْرِ بِمَوْتِي أَحَدٌ
sentences.tr: wa-illā muttu kamadan lam yadri bi-mawtī aḥadun
sentences.l: and-if-not I-died (of) grief, (and) not knew of-my-death anyone.”
sentences.i: or else I shall die of grief, and no one will know of my death.”
sentences.n: The print sets والا and متّ together, والامتّ; the spacing is kept and the word is read wa-illā muttu. wa-illā, “and if not, otherwise”, is in lā, “if not”, with the condition left unsaid; the perfect muttu after it has the future sense of a conditional answer. muttu, “I die”, from māta, the long ā giving way to short u before the ending; its shadda, the doubled t of mut-tu, is printed. kamadan, accusative of cause: kamad is grief kept hidden that eats at the heart. lam yadri, jussive of darā, “to know”, which takes bi- for what is known of, bi-mawtī, “of my death”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ أَظْهَرَ الْوَجْدَ وَالْتَفَتَ إِلَى أَبِيهِ وَأَنْشَدَ هٰذَيْنِ الْبَيْتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Qamara al-Zamāni aẓhara al-wajda wa-iltafata ilā abīhi wa-anshada hādhayni al-baytayni
sentences.l: Then indeed Qamar al-Zamān showed the-passion and-turned to his-father and-recited these-two the-two-verses:
sentences.i: Then Qamar al-Zamān let his passion show, turned to his father, and recited these two lines:
sentences.n: aẓhara, Form IV, “to show, let appear”. wajd, the passion of longing. anshada, Form IV, “to recite (verse)”. hādhayni al-baytayni, demonstrative and noun both in the dual and the accusative.

sentences.t:
اِنْ كَانَ وَعْدُكُمْ بِالْوَصْلِ تَزْوِيرُ * فَفِي الْكَرَى وَاصِلُوا الْمُشْتَاقَ اَوْ زُورُوا
قَالُوا وَكَيْفَ يَزُورُ الطَّيْفُ جَفْنَ فَتَى * مَنَامُهُ عَنْهُ مَمْنُوعٌ وَمَحْجُورُ
sentences.tr:
in kāna waʿdukum bi-al-waṣli tazwīru * fa-fī al-karā wāṣilū al-mushtāqa aw zūrū
qālū wa-kayfa yazūru al-ṭayfu jafna fatan * manāmuhu ʿanhu mamnūʿun wa-maḥjūru
sentences.l:
If was your-promise of-the-union a-forgery, * then-in the-slumber join the-longing-one, or visit!
They-said: And-how visits the-phantom (the) eyelid (of) a-youth * his-sleep from-him (is) forbidden and-barred?
sentences.i:
If your promise of union is a sham, * then in sleep come to him who longs for you, or visit him;
They said: And how shall a phantom visit the eyes of a youth * from whom all sleep is forbidden and barred?
sentences.n: The print points the verse, and its pointing is kept. After kāna Classical Arabic would have the accusative, tazwīran; the print gives tazwīru, keeping the rhyme in -ūru. tazwīr, “forgery, sham”, and zūrū, “visit!”, come from one root, z-w-r, a play the line is built on. The beloved is addressed in the plural (waʿdukum, wāṣilū, zūrū), a usual discretion of love poetry. waʿd bi-, “a promise of”: bi- marks what is promised. al-karā, “slumber”. al-ṭayf, “the phantom”, the image of the beloved that visits the lover in dreams, a stock figure of the love poem; the second line answers the first: a phantom can only come to one who sleeps. fatan is written فَتَى, with no mark of the tanwīn. manāmuhu ʿanhu mamnūʿun …, an unmarked relative clause describing the youth.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ بَعْدَ إِنْشَادِ هٰذِهِ الْأَشْعَارِ الْتَفَتَ إِلَى أَبِيهِ بِخُضُوعٍ وَانْكِسَارٍ وَأَفَاضَ الْعَبَرَاتِ وَأَنْشَدَ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Qamara al-Zamāni baʿda inshādi hādhihi al-ashʿāri iltafata ilā abīhi bi-khuḍūʿin wa-inkisārin wa-afāḍa al-ʿabarāti wa-anshada hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: Then indeed Qamar al-Zamān, after (the) reciting (of) these the-poems, turned to his-father with-submission and-brokenness, and-poured-out the-tears and-recited these the-verses:
sentences.i: Then, after reciting these lines, Qamar al-Zamān turned to his father humbly and brokenly, shed tears, and recited these verses:
sentences.n: inshād, verbal noun of anshada, “reciting”. bi-khuḍūʿin wa-inkisārin, “with humility and brokenness”, bi- of manner, in rhyme; inkisār, Form VII, “being broken”, of a crushed spirit. afāḍa, Form IV, “to make overflow”; ʿabarāt, “tears”. The verses he recites are not given before morning comes; they are never given; the next night takes up the story after them.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night.
